historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Benzodiazepines

starting.description: An empirical tranquilizer search yielded an unexpected animal pharmacology profile for the synthetic compound later named chlordiazepoxide; its promising effects prompted synthesis of related benzodiazepines.

inspiration.description: Unexpected sedative, muscle-relaxant and anticonvulsant animal effects of the synthetic chlordiazepoxide lead prompted further development. Upstream, natural alkaloids were among the examples behind a broad basic-amine design heuristic, alongside synthetic drugs; they were not identified as natural molecular precursors of the benzodiazepine lead.

steps.description: The group pursued a deliberate empirical chemical search for a new tranquilizer, selecting chemistry familiar from earlier dyestuff work.
An untested synthetic sample was submitted for pharmacological screening in 1957 and showed an unexpectedly promising animal-test profile; this effect motivated synthesis of analogues.
Structural investigation revealed that an unexpected chemical rearrangement had formed the 1,4-benzodiazepine ring; the active lead became chlordiazepoxide.
An active decomposition product and subsequent molecular modifications yielded diazepam, selected for higher potency in tests.

Upjohn researchers subsequently developed triazolobenzodiazepines by modifying the established 1,4-benzodiazepine system and testing the new compounds against diazepam analogues; the 1971 series included the compound later named alprazolam.

design.description: Researchers synthesized and screened the initial compound, elucidated and modified the active chemical series, and selected a more potent 1-methyl derivative for development as diazepam.

circumstances.description: The search for a tranquilizer and the 1957 animal screening were planned; the positive pharmacological result for the stored compound was unexpected.

limits: The two retrospectives are by the same discoverer and do not independently corroborate each other.

Sternbach distinguishes Roche's clonazepam from Wyeth's lorazepam as later analogues. Upjohn's alprazolam is a later triazolobenzodiazepine; its detailed internal research decisions are not reconstructed as a separate class founding.
The S7 review names all four assigned members as benzodiazepines (E17), but a shared class label does not establish each analogue's complete genealogy.
conflicts: The 2005 review S7 describes chlordiazepoxide as emerging from side-chain work within chlorpromazine's structure (E14). Sternbach's oral history instead distinguishes an earlier unproductive phenothiazine effort from his later intention to seek a new group unrelated to Thorazine (E15). The extent of structural analogy or direct influence is unresolved; the supported observation-led judgment rests on the subsequent tested lead and its documented development, not on deciding this upstream disagreement.
gaps: The 1960 original pharmacology report was read only as the publisher's abstract, not in full; the original 1957 screening records have not been located.
The specific internal decisions producing the Upjohn compound are not established by the later statement that its activity prompted additional analogues.
